title: Review: Capacitance and capacitor energy; Electric field strength and field lines; Capacitor charging and discharging; Springs and Hooke's law; Stress, strain and Young modulus
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: D06-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; F03-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; EL09-3#t3 term and clue written for the game; D06-1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: D06-1#N.2b, EL09-3#N.4, EL10-1#N.4b, F03-1#N.11, MT01-1#N.9, D06-1#N.12, EL10-1#N.8, F03-1#N.2, MT01-1#N.6. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Extension
items.clue: Stretched length minus the original length, not the whole length.

items.label: Neutral point
items.clue: Place between two like charges where E = 0, nearer the smaller one.

items.label: Isolated conductor
items.clue: What two joined inner plates form, so their net charge cannot change.

items.label: Compression
items.clue: Squashing a spring, where the change counted is the decrease in length.

questions.stem: In a lab, a student models a spring as a light spring that obeys Hooke's law. Which statement describes how the spring's force behaves in this model?

options.text: Its force is proportional to its length, measured end to end.
Its force doubles when its extension doubles.
Its force is the same however far it is stretched or compressed.
Its force depends on how fast the attached object is moving.

questions.stem: Four identical capacitors, each of capacitance C, are first connected all in parallel, giving an equivalent capacitance C_X. They are then reconnected all in series, giving an equivalent capacitance C_Y. How does C_X compare with C_Y?

options.text: C_X is the same as C_Y.

questions.stem: A capacitor is charged through a resistor by a battery. At time t₁ the p.d. across the capacitor is one quarter of the battery's emf. At a later time t₂ it is three quarters of the emf. What is the current at t₂ divided by the current at t₁?
questions.explanation: Current = (p.d. across the resistor) ÷ R. At t₁ that p.d. is ¾ of the emf; at t₂ it is ¼. Ratio: ¼ ÷ ¾ = 1/3.

questions.stem: The field lines of a long, straight charged wire spread out radially, in planes at right angles to the wire: they spread in two dimensions, not three. Point P is 2.0 cm from the wire and point Q is 6.0 cm from it, both far from the wire's ends. How does the electric field strength at P compare with that at Q?

options.text: E at P is 9 times E at Q, as the field strength falls with the square of the distance.
E at P is 3 times E at Q, as the same lines spread over 3 times the area at Q.
E is the same at P and Q, as every line that passes P also passes Q.
E at Q is 3 times E at P, as the larger cylinder at Q holds more lines.

questions.stem: Two cables are made of the same aluminium alloy and carry the same load. Cable Q is 3 times as long as cable P and has 3 times its diameter. Both obey Hooke's law. What is the extension of Q divided by the extension of P?
questions.explanation: Extension = force × length ÷ (area × Young modulus). Same force and material; length × 3; area × 3² = 9. Ratio = 3/9 = 1/3.

questions.stem: A spring that obeys Hooke's law is 15.0 cm long when it supports a 3.0 N load and 18.0 cm long when it supports a 6.0 N load. What is its natural (unloaded) length?
questions.explanation: The extra 3.0 N adds 3.0 cm, so the extension is 1.0 cm per newton. With 3.0 N on, the extension is 3.0 cm: natural length = 15.0 − 3.0 = 12.0 cm.

questions.stem: An uncharged capacitor is charged through a 3.0 kΩ resistor by an ideal battery of emf 9.0 V, all connected in series. What is the current in the resistor at the instant when the potential difference across the capacitor is 6.0 V?

At point P, a charge of +2.0 µC experiences an electric force of 5.0 × 10⁻³ N directed east. This charge is removed and a charge of −6.0 µC is placed at P; the charges that produce the field do not move. Taking east as positive, what is the electric force on the −6.0 µC charge?

A student repeats the Young modulus experiment with the same loads on a wire of the same metal and diameter, but only one tenth as long. The extension is read with the same scale. What is the main effect?

options.text: Each extension is ten times smaller, so its percentage uncertainty is ten times larger.
The Young modulus found is ten times smaller.
The stress is ten times larger, so the wire passes its limit of proportionality.
Nothing changes, as the Young modulus is a property of the material.

questions.explanation: Strain is unchanged, so extension ∝ original length. The same reading error is now ten times larger as a fraction of the extension.
